book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!

chapters.relation: Piven argues that evil in the story runs from the overt villains to the beloved heroes: Humperdinck's rage at Westley is analyzed as malignant envy of true love, Rugen's torture as dispassionate sadistic curiosity, and Vizzini's pompous moralizing as narcissistic hypocrisy masking childhood shame and nightmares. He applies Hannah Arendt's banality of evil to Inigo and Fezzik, who soberly assault and abduct Buttercup, and then brands Westley - a pirate who admits he liked piracy and who slaps and strangles Buttercup to test her fidelity - as possibly the evilest character, likening his love-justified slaughter to the terrorist's logic. The point is that we adore these characters only by ignoring deeds we would condemn in real life.

chapters.file: ch27 - 14. The End of Inigo Montoya.md
chapters.relation: Elsby and Luzecky read Inigo through Aristotle's doctrine of the four causes: his life is organized by a final cause, revenge on the Six-Fingered Man as the thing that is 'just good', which explains every action from fencing drills to eating breakfast. The famous mantra works because habit embodies the final cause - repeating 'My name is Inigo Montoya' lets trained movement carry him through wounds that should end the fight. When revenge is achieved the chain of ends terminates and 'Inigo Montoya' ends with it, which is why his rebirth as the Dread Pirate Roberts is needed; the chapter generalizes that our habits, not grand outside purposes, are how final causes give lives their ends.

chapters.file: ch28 - 15. It Would Take a Miracle!.md
chapters.relation: Barkman and Käärid ask whether Miracle Max's revival of 'mostly dead' Westley is a miracle, staging David Hume - for whom a violation of natural law is never more credible than mistaken or lying testimony, so Hume in Florin would call Max a deceiver and Inigo and Fezzik barbarous dupes - against C.S. Lewis, for whom a miracle is a new, unpredictable element introduced into nature rather than a violation of it. They add puzzles neither philosopher addresses: whether Westley was truly dead, whether a 'rotten miracle' would still count, and why Max's miracles seem to require 'unshattered' confidence, concluding that Florin's miracles are person-dependent in a way Hume's skepticism and Lewis's supernaturalism both miss.

chapters.file: ch29 - 16. My Name Is—Hang on, What Was It Meant to Be Again Are You Sure Well, Okay Then . ..md
chapters.relation: Tim Jones argues the book is not really a love story but a warning about identity: against Descartes's transcendent self, the American pragmatists William James, Cooley, and Mead hold that the self is fluid and socially constituted, and Westley's serial reinvention (farm boy, Dread Pirate Roberts, Man in Black) - along with Mandy Patinkin's cathartic channeling of his father's death into Inigo - shows the freedom this mutability grants. The Goldman frame then exposes the danger: the fictionalized Goldman seizes Morgenstern's text, cuts its history, and rewrites it to his own ends, exactly as other people can seize our plastic identities and shape them for their interests rather than ours.

chapters.file: ch30 - 17. The Miracle of True Love.md
chapters.relation: Elsby and Luzecky use the Phaedo to make sense of Westley being 'mostly dead': Socrates's cyclical argument that opposites generate each other, Aristotle's distinctions between contradictories and contraries, and the observation that life and death here come in degrees together recast life and death as spectrum concepts rather than strict opposites. True love emerges as a second opposite of death: answering Simmias's objection that a soul, like a lyre's harmony, perishes with its instrument, they argue true love is a harmony binding persons and actions that persists beyond the particular lovers - which is how the film's miracle of true love conquers death.

chapters.file: ch31 - Part V Life Lessons of a Fairytale.md
ch32 - 18. I Know Something You Don’t Know.md
chapters.relation: Auxier argues the three contests turn on loyalty rather than morality: Josiah Royce's account of life's meaning as devoted service to a chosen cause explains the fair play of the duels on the Cliffs of Insanity, Inigo's and Fezzik's artistry, why Westley spares them 'for the sake of art, not goodness', and why Vizzini, Rugen, and Humperdinck, who serve only their own twisted egos, get no sporting chance. He reads Westley and Buttercup's love as a shared cause whose loss should have been morally educative (Royce on lost causes), faults passive Buttercup and pirate-playing Westley for failing to grow through it, and closes with Royce's 'loyalty to loyalty' as the meaning of the swordfight's mutual admiration and of Inigo's final act of mercy.

chapters.file: ch33 - 19. The Medical Ethics of Miracle Max.md
chapters.relation: Shea treats Miracle Max as a one-man healthcare system to teach biomedical ethics: Max's lies about Valerie the 'witch', the fee, and the pill's duration violate the principle of autonomy and informed consent; the withholding-versus-withdrawing of the miracle pill and hypothetical Zoo of Death experiments engage nonmaleficence; his price and his duty to a mostly-dead stranger by the road raise beneficence; and who deserves resurrection under a monopoly raises justice, weighed across libertarian, utilitarian, and liberal-egalitarian (worst-off-maximizing) answers. The chapter concludes that principlism's four principles handle such dilemmas better than any single mechanical rule.

chapters.file: ch34 - 20. The Good and the Gracious.md
chapters.relation: Olson and Taliaferro read manners as the story's moral barometer: the genuine, effusive compliments exchanged by Westley and Inigo atop the Cliffs of Insanity, and Fezzik's sporting wrestling, express care and connection, while Humperdinck's and Rugen's courtly politeness is camouflage for torture, murder, and war. Against Machiavelli's instrumental use of courtesy in The Prince, they recruit Plato's sophrosyne as 'good form' inseparable from justice, wisdom, and courage, and Confucian li as etiquette that instructs and steadies us toward virtue, with Hobbes's 'small morals' marking the hollow version; they add that manners also police class, from Buttercup's 'Farm Boy' to reality TV and the financiers of the Great Recession who used the correct fork.

chapters.file: ch35 - 21. Buttercup and the Eternal Feminine.md
chapters.relation: Archibald reads Buttercup wholly through Beauvoir's The Second Sex: as the farm's natural leader she is not yet 'woman as Other', but Humperdinck's ultra-feminized public presentation, the arranged marriage, the old woman's 'Queen of Filth' nightmare, and the men dismissing her advice all enact the myth of the eternal feminine that punishes a woman for asserting herself. Her leap toward the shrieking eels becomes an emblem of autonomy that society punishes, the 'privilege' of compliance a curse that leaves her suicidal, and the closing image of the couple riding together as one sketches Beauvoir's ideal of a relationship founded on mutual liberty.

chapters.file: ch36 - 22. The Dao of Master Westley.md
chapters.relation: Doll tests each character against the Dao: Confucius's identification of the Dao with tradition and ritual fails because Florinese tradition is exactly what enables Humperdinck's murder and war plans, so she turns to Laozi's De and wu-wei, diagnosing Vizzini's fatal overconfidence (he lacked Socratic knowledge of his own ignorance), Humperdinck's paranoia, and Buttercup's passivity as failures to sense when to act and when to refrain. Westley emerges as Zhuangzi's ideal - like Cook Ting the butcher, mastering skills until instinct suffices: adapting through the Fire Swamp, treating Vizzini's death as 'an appropriate death', yet sparing Inigo and Fezzik because killing them would be against nature, which is why the giant and the Spaniard accept him as their sage.

chapters.file: ch37 - 23. Why No One Would Surrender to the Dread Pirate Westley.md
chapters.relation: Clint Jones argues the Dread Pirate Roberts is Florinese cultural mythology rather than a man: like Billy the Kid or the Cowboy myth, the name carries a symbolic identity that lets Westley reinvent himself ('no one would surrender to the Dread Pirate Westley'), explains why only Buttercup, raised on Florin's stories, recognizes the Man in Black while the well-traveled Inigo, Fezzik, and Vizzini cannot, and why the palace guards panic at Fezzik in the Holocaust Cloak. Humperdinck figures as Hobbes's Leviathan, the embodiment of the state whose war with Guilder would shore up a Florinese identity destabilized by the New World, while Derrida's Politics of Friendship supplies the logic that a stable 'we' requires a clearly marked enemy.

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Christian apologist and novelist whose book Miracles defends supernaturalism, treating a miracle as God introducing a new element into the regular stream of nature rather than violating natural law.
holes.why: Chapter 28's entire debate over Miracle Max's miracle pairs Hume's skepticism against Lewis's supernaturalism, and half its argument cannot be indexed without him.

holes.name: Josiah Royce
holes.what: American idealist philosopher whose The Philosophy of Loyalty grounds the meaning of life in loyal service to freely chosen causes and in being 'loyal to loyalty itself'.
holes.why: Chapter 32 is built on Royce's philosophy of loyalty to explain the duelists' fair play, honor among thieves, lost causes, and why Westley's conduct satisfies though it is not precisely moral.

holes.name: The Philosophy of Loyalty
holes.what: Royce's view that a self comes into existence through willing, habitual service to a cause, that lost causes can be idealized into moral growth, and that loyalty itself deserves loyalty.
holes.why: Chapter 32 applies loyalty, loyalty's training through sport, and lost-cause idealization to Inigo, Fezzik, Westley, and Buttercup, and no existing taxonomy slug covers loyalty.

holes.name: Principlism (Four Principles of Biomedical Ethics)
holes.what: Beauchamp and Childress's framework grounding medical ethics in four balancing principles: autonomy, nonmaleficence, beneficence, and justice.
holes.why: Chapter 33 is structured entirely around applying the four principles to Miracle Max's treatment of Westley, and taxonomy has no slug for principlism or biomedical principles.

holes.name: Joseph Campbell
holes.what: Comparative mythologist whose account of myth as the support of civilizations, moral orders, and cultural identity is the chapter's main authority.
holes.why: Chapter 37 quotes Campbell repeatedly to ground its claim that the Dread Pirate Roberts legend sustains Florinese cultural identity, and he is absent from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Cultural Mythology (myth as social identity)
holes.what: The idea, developed by Joseph Campbell, Jerome Bruner, and Karen Armstrong, that shared myths supply a culture's identity, cohesion, and moral order and are updated rather than discarded.
holes.why: Chapter 37's central claim is that the Dread Pirate Roberts functions as the mythology of Florin's cultural identity, and no existing slug captures that concept.
